title: Your pre-trade checklist
desc: Run 5 to 7 yes/no checks before every trade; one “no” means no trade

cards.title: Why a checklist?
cards.situation: Pilots run a checklist before every flight, even after 10,000 flights. Why should a trader use one?

options.feedback: A checklist doesn’t replace your rules. It checks you follow them. Experience doesn’t stop mistakes. It makes people skip steps.

options.text: It catches rushed trades and missed steps
options.feedback: A checklist slows you down for one minute at the moment you’re most likely to rush.

options.text: It makes every trade a winner
options.feedback: No checklist makes every trade a winner. It stops rushed trades and skipped steps.

cards.work: 6 yes/no checks take about a minute. One “no” saves a bad trade.

cards.title: 5 to 7 yes/no checks
cards.text: Before every trade you run a short **[[pre-trade-checklist|checklist]]**. Each check is a fact you can answer yes or no.

items.text: It’s one of my markets and my style
My stop is set before I buy
My target is at least 2× the risk
I’m inside my daily and weekly limits

cards.title: Run a real setup
cards.text: Entry $40, stop $38. Resistance sits at $42, so your target is $42: risk $2 to make $2.

items.text: It’s one of my markets and my style
My stop is set before I buy
My target is at least 2× the risk
I’m inside my daily and weekly limits

blocks.tip: Don’t squeeze the stop to fix the numbers. The stop goes where you’re wrong.

cards.foot: Target only 1× the risk. One “no”, so you skip it and wait for a better setup.

cards.title: Too good for a checklist?
cards.myth: Experienced traders don’t need a checklist.
cards.reality: The checklist matters most on bad days: tired, angry or chasing a loss. That’s when people skip steps.

cards.title: A good check
cards.q: Which one belongs on your yes/no checklist?

options.text: Is the stock likely to go up?
options.feedback: “Likely to go up” is a guess, and the answer is always yes. A check must be a fact, like whether the stop is set.

options.text: Is my stop set before I buy?
options.feedback: It’s a fact you can answer yes or no in a second. That’s what a check should be.
“Great company” is an opinion. A check must be a fact you can answer yes or no.
What people talk about is noise. A check must be a fact about your own plan.

cards.title: Five yes, one no
cards.q: Five checks say yes. One says no: the trade would take you past your weekly loss limit. What now?

options.text: Take it: 5 of 6 is good enough
options.feedback: A checklist isn’t a score. One “no” means no trade, and a loss limit never bends.

options.text: Skip it: one “no” means no trade
options.feedback: One “no” means no trade. Your weekly limit never bends, so you wait for next week.
Double size past your weekly limit makes the damage bigger. One “no” means no trade.
A limit you raise when you hit it was never a limit. One “no” means no trade.

cards.headline: You check before you click.
lines: Each check is a fact, not a feeling.
